clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive demyelinating CMT whose hallmark is early-onset and frequently severe scoliosis.
Spinal deformity may dominate the presentation and can precede overt limb weakness, so the neuropathy is sometimes recognised late.
Cranial nerve involvement, including facial weakness, tongue involvement and sensorineural hearing loss, is a recognised feature.
One of the commonest causes of autosomal recessive demyelinating CMT, with high frequency reported in Roma and Mediterranean populations.
Nerve conduction shows demyelinating slowing, and biopsy demonstrates onion-bulb formation with axonal loss.
Caused by biallelic SH3TC2 mutations that impair Schwann cell myelination and endosomal recycling.
Regular spinal surveillance is essential given the deformity burden and its respiratory consequences.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4C is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in SH3TC2 (also known as KIAA1985), which encodes a protein containing SH3 and tetratricopeptide repeat domains that is highly expressed in Schwann cells. The protein localises to the endosomal recycling compartment and plasma membrane and interacts with Rab11, linking it to membrane recycling required for the enormous surface expansion of myelinating Schwann cells. Loss of functional SH3TC2 disrupts Schwann cell myelin formation and maintenance, producing an early-onset demyelinating neuropathy with secondary axonal degeneration. The particular vulnerability of paraspinal innervation and the timing of onset are thought to underlie the prominent, early scoliosis that distinguishes this subtype.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of early-onset scoliosis with a peripheral neuropathy
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy in childhood
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography confirming demyelinating slowing
SH3TC2 sequencing within a hereditary neuropathy gene panel
Spinal radiographs and orthopaedic review for scoliosis progression
Audiometry to detect sensorineural hearing loss
Sural nerve biopsy in diagnostically unclear cases
redFlags: Progressive scoliosis with restrictive respiratory compromise
New or worsening sensorineural hearing loss
Bulbar or other cranial nerve signs
Rapid neurological deterioration suggesting an acquired process
reference.prognosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4C progresses slowly at the level of the neuropathy and ambulation is often preserved into adulthood, but the early scoliosis and cranial nerve involvement add considerable disability and may threaten respiratory function.
pitfalls: Attributing scoliosis to an idiopathic cause and missing the underlying hereditary neuropathy.
Failing to screen for hearing loss and cranial nerve involvement.
Not considering a recessive diagnosis in an apparently isolated case, especially with consanguinity.
Delaying spinal monitoring so that curve progression outpaces intervention.
